items.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: In fact, when we do the Garrison Keillor show, we’re playing music from that era

ctx.x: What do you think about taking music like that, that was written in the ’30s and arranged in the ’30s – how do you as a musician approach music that you heard in its original form but are playing today in 1992? What’s your own approach?

There are different types of phrasings. You try to play – you can play – they’re the same notes, but you can just change the phrasing so that it sounds more modern than what it did in those days. I wish I could think of an example. Say [Wilder sings a brief phrase] something like that. In the old days, they might have played [he sings it again]. They’d play like that. In the phrasing today, they would try it smoothly, play a little more smoothly [he sings it with one note flowing into the next] or something like…
So really it’s the phrasing that gives it the era.
